tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 600000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.description:

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

### Triage mode

For an unclear request, perform read-only examination first. Report the

### Administration mode

For explicit operational administration, inspect status, validate packets,

report the capability gap and stop before unsafe mutation.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

schema.name: Skill
schema.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Use the shared [workflow terminology](../../AGENTS.md#workflow-terminology).

# Spec Research & Authoring

Deploy a parallel research team to investigate requirements for a new spec, then synthesize findings into a complete feature specification document. The research phase uses 3 subagents with distinct investigation angles to ensure comprehensive coverage before writing begins.

## Arguments

Accept a spec topic or folder path (e.g., `notifications`, `feature-007`, `docs/notifications/`, or a plain description like "real-time notifications system").  
If a stub README already exists in the feature folder (for example `docs/feature-name/README.md`), read it for initial scope constraints.

## Time budget and checkpoint

At entry, before each numbered task or phase, after a lengthy direct operation,
and immediately before and after each worker dispatch or blocking wait, run
`python "/Users/gkhoo-c/.Projects/mxc-c0/work/.eval-cfg-20261102T053248Z/plugin/geeky-orchestration/scripts/workflow-budget.py" --stage spec-research --json`.
Resolve `/Users/gkhoo-c/.Projects/mxc-c0/work/.eval-cfg-20261102T053248Z/plugin/geeky-orchestration` to the installed plugin root containing this skill
when the environment variable is unset, and use an available Python interpreter.
If the helper cannot run or its output is unreadable, stop and report the missing
budget check; do not assume unlimited time. Read the JSON status, not just the
exit code: `unbounded` means no deadline was provided; `active` continues; `reserve` or `exhausted` stops starting new work
and checkpoints the incomplete stage; `invalid` stops and reports the configuration
error. A zero exit also covers `reserve`, so it is not permission to continue.
The stage target is advisory, not a gate or guarantee: after it is exceeded,
finish required work with the smallest sufficient evidence and defer optional
expansion. Never skip a required review, validator or acceptance condition, or
claim an incomplete stage passed. Pass the hard deadline, closeout reserve, and
stage target from the check to every child brief. If the deadline is absent, say
unbounded; if only the target is absent, say the target is unavailable. Do not
invent either value. Tell each child to return its current evidence,
unresolved questions and status before the available work time ends. Bound waits by
the remaining usable time where the host supports it; if it cannot, record that
limitation rather than claiming cancellation. Recheck after a wait; a child report alone does not override the budget result.

If the budget stops this stage, preserve completed research and note missing evidence; do not declare the spec complete or start planning as if it passed.

## Workflow

### Phase 1: Scope Discovery

Before dispatching researchers:

1. Determine the feature folder name. If the argument is already a folder path, use it. Otherwise derive `docs/spec-NNN-<kebab-slug>/`: read `CLAUDE.md` `## Current State` for the current sequence if present. If `CLAUDE.md` is missing, malformed, or the `## Current State` section is absent, continue with fallback naming logic: list existing `docs/spec-*` folders and use the highest number + 1. If no numbered folders exist, follow whatever folder convention prior specs in `docs/` use; if `docs/` is empty, ask the user to confirm the folder name before proceeding.
2. Read any existing stub (`docs/<folder>/README.md`) for scope constraints.
3. Scan the codebase for existing patterns and integration points.
4. Identify 3 distinct research angles based on what the feature needs to cover.

### Phase 2: Define 3 Research Angles

Select 3 non-overlapping research angles based on the feature domain. Each agent investigates a different facet.

Typical per-domain configurations (infrastructure / domain-feature / security-compliance, always anchored by a Codebase Analyst) are in `references/research-angle-menus.md` — load it when picking the angles.

### Phase 3: Dispatch Research Team in Parallel

Deploy all 3 researchers simultaneously.

- **Codebase Analyst**: use `geeky-orchestration:code-explorer` agent type.
- **Web Researchers (2)**: use `general-purpose` agent type with instructions to use `WebSearch` and `WebFetch`.

Give each researcher specific questions and source boundaries. Use the provided contract and existing authoritative evidence first; fetch further sources only to resolve a material requirement, uncertainty, or contradiction. Stop searching once those questions are answered. Each report should be concise and source-linked, with unresolved gaps stated explicitly. Avoid duplicate source collection across angles.

Each research brief ends with:

```
Produce a structured report with:
- Key findings (numbered, specific)
- Constraints discovered (what the spec MUST respect)
- Recommendations (what the spec SHOULD include)
- Sources (URLs for web research, file paths for codebase)

DO NOT create or modify any files.
```

### Phase 4: Synthesize into Spec Document

After all 3 researchers report back:

1. Consolidate findings: merge overlap, resolve contradictions, and note confidence gaps.
2. Define scope: goals, non-goals, delegation items.
3. Write the requirements document using the project’s established conventions in:
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/feature-specification.md`
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/README.md`

   Do not create `SPEC-NNNN-*.md` files — that naming is legacy; `feature-specification.md` is the canonical filename consumed by /geeky-plan and the freeze hooks.

   If a stub README already exists, preserve its stated scope and only update the Status line and missing sections; otherwise create the README stub:

   ```markdown
   # [Feature Name]

   [One-paragraph scope summary.]

   **Status:** Spec written — not yet planned
   **Spec:** `feature-specification.md`
   **Next:** /geeky-plan docs/<feature-folder>/
   ```

Use the 11-section recommended spec structure in `references/spec-structure-template.md` (adapt sections to the feature domain; include citations and explicit assumptions at the end of major findings).

### Phase 5: Commit and Suggest Next Steps

Commit the spec (same command on all platforms). The spec is not yet frozen — it only becomes part of the frozen planning contract after /geeky-plan runs:

```
git add docs/<feature-folder>/
git commit -m "docs: author feature specification in <feature-folder>" -m "[1-line summary of the spec focus]" -m "Research conducted by: codebase analyst, researcher 2 domain, researcher 3 domain" -m "Tasks: none (pre-planning specification)"
```

Then suggest next steps:
```
Spec written. Next steps:
- /geeky-plan docs/<feature-folder>/   (to create implementation plan, tasks, kanban)
- /plan-review docs/<feature-folder>/  (to validate the planning package)
- /geeky-implement docs/<feature-folder>/ (to execute)
```

## Research Quality Standards

- **Recency**: Target sources from roughly the past 18 months; avoid older sources unless they cover stable fundamentals.
- **Authority**: Prefer official documentation (Microsoft Learn, AWS docs, RFC specs) over blogs or forums.
- **Specificity**: Include concrete findings (resource types, API versions, package versions, pricing tiers).
- **Adversarial verification**: If researchers disagree on a fact, preserve both positions and flag for user decision.

## Rules

- **Always 3 researchers** — one codebase analyst + two web/domain researchers.
- **Parallel dispatch** — all 3 in a single turn for maximum speed.
- **Research before writing** — do not start the spec document until all researchers report back.
- **Cite sources** — every major claim in the spec should trace to research.
- **Respect existing stubs** — if a README stub exists, treat its stated scope as authoritative unless research justifies adjustments.
- **Follow project conventions** — spec format, naming, and folder structure should match prior specs in `docs/`.

Use only the Python 3.11+ standard library: `http.server` for the server and `sqlite3` for storage; pytest is allowed for your own tests. An admin key issues bearer tokens, and each token can create, list, inspect and delete only its own short links. Short links redirect with HTTP 302, can carry an optional custom slug and expiry, and count their clicks. Each token is rate-limited, and all data except rate-limit counters survives a server restart. The server binds 127.0.0.1 only, prints one ready line, supports a fake clock for testing, and shuts down cleanly on Ctrl+C on Windows, macOS and Linux. Follow `contract.md` exactly, because an automated test suite checks status codes, JSON keys and key order, headers, output and exit codes. Keep the code minimal and readable, and include tests for the behaviour you build.

1	Build `linkvault`, a small URL-shortener HTTP JSON API with a command-line client, in the `linkvault/` package at the root of this workspace. Use only the Python 3.11+ standard library: `http.server` for the server and `sqlite3` for storage; pytest is allowed for your own tests. An admin key issues bearer tokens, and each token can create, list, inspect and delete only its own short links. Short links redirect with HTTP 302, can carry an optional custom slug and expiry, and count their clicks. Each token is rate-limited, and all data except rate-limit counters survives a server restart. The server binds 127.0.0.1 only, prints one ready line, supports a fake clock for testing, and shuts down cleanly on Ctrl+C on Windows, macOS and Linux. Follow `contract.md` exactly, because an automated test suite checks status codes, JSON keys and key order, headers, output and exit codes. Keep the code minimal and readable, and include tests for the behaviour you build.
2

1	# linkvault: Interface Contract
2	
3	## Constraints
4	
5	- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, stdlib only (`http.server`, `sqlite3`, `json`, `argparse`, `urllib`, `secrets`, `hashlib`, `threading`, `signal`); pytest for tests only.
6	- **Package location:** `linkvault/` at the workspace root (`linkvault/__init__.py`, `linkvault/__main__.py`); commands run with the workspace root as cwd.
7	- **Entry points:** `python -m linkvault serve ...` (server); `python -m linkvault <client-cmd> ...` (client).
8	
9	## Functional requirements
10	
11	- **R1 Server start.** `serve` opens or creates the DB, binds 127.0.0.1, then prints exactly one ready line to stdout. Nothing else is ever written to stdout; logs go to stderr.
12	- **R2 Token issuance.** `POST /v1/tokens` with the correct admin key returns a new token. The token is `lv_` followed by 32 lowercase hex characters (`secrets.token_hex(16)`). Only its SHA-256 hex digest is stored.
13	- **R3 Authentication.** Every `/v1/links` route requires `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A missing, malformed or unknown token returns 401.
14	- **R4 Create link.** `POST /v1/links` stores `url` with a custom `slug` or a generated slug, and an optional `expires_in`.
15	- **R5 Slug rules.** Slugs are case-sensitive. A custom slug must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,32}$` and must not be `healthz`. A generated slug is 7 characters from `abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789`, drawn with `secrets.choice`. It is regenerated if it already exists or is reserved, with up to 5 attempts and then 500. Creating an existing slug returns 409.
16	- **R6 URL rules.** The scheme is `http` or `https` (case-insensitive). `urllib.parse.urlsplit(url).hostname` is non-empty. The URL is at most 2048 characters and contains no whitespace or control characters (code points < 0x21 or 0x7F). It is stored and redirected to verbatim.
17	- **R7 Resolve.** `GET /<slug>` returns 302 with `Location: <url>` and an empty body. It atomically increments `clicks` and sets `last_clicked_at` to now.
18	- **R8 Missing and expired links.** An unknown slug returns 404. A link with `now >= expires_at` returns 410 and its click count is unchanged. Comparisons use whole seconds.
19	- **R9 List and inspect.** A token can list its own links (expired ones included) and fetch one link with its stats. Another token's link always returns 404, never 403.
20	- **R10 Delete.** A token can delete its own link. Afterwards the slug resolves 404 and is free to reuse.
21	- **R11 Rate limit.** Requests are counted per token in fixed 60-second windows aligned to the Unix epoch (`window_start = now - now % 60`). The limit is `--rate-limit` (default 60) counted requests per window. A request is counted when it reaches the rate-limit step (see precedence in Error handling), whatever its final status. Request number `limit + 1` and later in the same window return 429 with `Retry-After: <window_start + 60 - now>`. Counters are in memory and reset on restart. Redirects, `/healthz` and admin routes are not rate-limited.
22	- **R12 Clock.** "Now" is integer Unix seconds (floor of real time). With `--fake-clock <ISO>`, now is frozen at that instant and changes only through `POST /v1/admin/clock`. The fake clock is not persisted.
23	- **R13 Persistence.** Tokens, links, clicks and `last_clicked_at` survive a restart on the same `--db`.
24	- **R14 Concurrency.** The server is a `ThreadingHTTPServer`. N concurrent redirects to one slug leave `clicks == N` exactly.
25	- **R15 Shutdown.** On SIGINT, SIGTERM (POSIX) or CTRL_BREAK_EVENT/SIGBREAK (Windows), the server stops accepting connections, closes the DB and exits 0 within 5 seconds.
26	- **R16 Client.** CLI commands wrap the API. Each prints the response body to stdout, and uses the exit codes below.
27	
28	## Interface contract
29	
30	### Conventions
31	
32	- Timestamps are `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ` in UTC with whole seconds. They are stored as INTEGER Unix seconds.
33	- JSON responses are encoded with `json.dumps(obj, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=True)` in UTF-8, with `Content-Type: application/json`. Every response sets `Content-Length`; a 204 response has an empty body and MUST send `Content-Length: 0`. Keys appear in exactly the order listed below.
34	- Request `Content-Type` is ignored. The body is read using `Content-Length` (absent means empty), and the maximum is 8192 bytes.
35	- Query strings are ignored on every route. Paths are matched exactly, with no trailing-slash normalisation. Any (method, path) pair not listed below returns 404 `not_found`.
36	- `short_url` is `http://127.0.0.1:<bound port>/<slug>`.
37	
38	**Link object** (key order is fixed): `{"slug", "url", "short_url", "created_at", "expires_at", "clicks", "last_clicked_at"}`. `expires_at` and `last_clicked_at` are `null` until they are set.
39	
40	### Server CLI
41	
42	```
43	python -m linkvault serve --db PATH --admin-key KEY [--port N] [--rate-limit N] [--fake-clock ISO]
44	```
45	
46	| Flag | Rule |
47	|---|---|
48	| `--db` | Required. The file is created if missing, and its parent directory must exist. |
49	| `--admin-key` | Required. Non-empty string. |
50	| `--port` | 0-65535, default 8000. The value 0 binds an OS-chosen free port. |
51	| `--rate-limit` | Integer >= 1, default 60. |
52	| `--fake-clock` | An ISO timestamp in the format above. It enables the admin clock route. |
53	
54	Ready line: `LISTENING http://127.0.0.1:<port>` followed by a line terminator, which may be `\n` or `\r\n`. It uses the actual bound port, is flushed immediately, and nothing else is written to stdout before it.
55	
56	Exit codes: 0 for a clean shutdown; 2 for a usage error (argparse); 3 if the port cannot be bound or the DB cannot be opened, with a message to stderr.
57	
58	### Endpoints
59	
60	| # | Method and path | Auth | Request body | Success response |
61	|---|---|---|---|---|
62	| E1 | `GET /healthz` | none | none | 200 `{"status":"ok"}` |
63	| E2 | `POST /v1/tokens` | `X-Admin-Key: <key>` | ignored | 201 `{"token":"lv_…","created_at":"…"}` |
64	| E3 | `POST /v1/links` | Bearer | `{"url": str, "slug"?: str, "expires_in"?: int}` | 201, link object |
65	| E4 | `GET /v1/links` | Bearer | none | 200 `{"links":[link…]}` ordered by `created_at` ascending, then `slug` ascending |
66	| E5 | `GET /v1/links/<slug>` | Bearer | none | 200, link object |
67	| E6 | `DELETE /v1/links/<slug>` | Bearer | none | 204, empty body |
68	| E7 | `GET /<slug>` | none | none | 302, `Location: <url>`, `Content-Length: 0`, empty body |
69	| E8 | `POST /v1/admin/clock` | `X-Admin-Key` | `{"now": ISO}` | 200 `{"now":"…"}`. The route exists only with `--fake-clock`; otherwise it returns 404. Any valid timestamp is accepted. |
70	
71	E3 body rules:
72	- The body is a JSON object with no extra keys.
73	- `url` is required and must follow R6.
74	- `slug` is optional and must follow R5. An explicit `null` is `invalid_request` (400).
75	- `expires_in` is optional. It is an integer from 1 to 31536000, and `bool` values are rejected. An explicit `null` is `invalid_request` (400). It sets `expires_at = created_at + expires_in`.
76	
77	E8 body rules:
78	- The body must be exactly `{"now": ISO}`, where ISO is a string in the timestamp format above.
79	- A missing `now` key, an extra key, a wrong type or an unparseable timestamp returns 400 `invalid_request`.
80	
81	A wrong or missing admin key on E2 or E8 returns 401. On E5, E6 and E7, a `<slug>` that fails `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,32}$` is a route mismatch, so it returns 404 at the route step, before auth.
82	
83	### DB schema (exact)
84	
85	```sql
86	PRAGMA user_version = 1;
87	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tokens (
88	  token_hash TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
89	  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL);
90	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS links (
91	  slug TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
92	  url TEXT NOT NULL,
93	  token_hash TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES tokens(token_hash),
94	  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
95	  expires_at INTEGER,
96	  clicks INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
97	  last_clicked_at INTEGER);
98	```
99	
100	A click is recorded with one statement: `UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1, last_clicked_at = ? WHERE slug = ?`.
101	
102	### Client CLI
103	
104	The server URL comes from `--server URL`, or else the `LINKVAULT_SERVER` environment variable. The token comes from `--token T`, or else `LINKVAULT_TOKEN`. Both options are accepted after the subcommand.
105	
106	| Command | Calls | Stdout on success |
107	|---|---|---|
108	| `token create --admin-key K` | E2 | Response JSON, one line |
109	| `shorten URL [--slug S] [--expires-in N]` | E3 | Response JSON, one line |
110	| `list` | E4 | Response JSON, one line |
111	| `stats SLUG` | E5 | Response JSON, one line |
112	| `delete SLUG` | E6 | Nothing |
113	
114	Output is re-serialised with the server's `json.dumps` settings and ends with `\n`. Client exit codes:
115	
116	| Code | Meaning | Output |
117	|---|---|---|
118	| 0 | 2xx response | as above |
119	| 1 | non-2xx response | Error JSON on stderr, stdout empty |
120	| 2 | usage error, or a missing server or token | Message on stderr |
121	| 3 | connection failure | Message on stderr |
122	
123	## Error handling
124	
125	Every error body has this shape: `{"error":{"code":"<code>","message":"<text>"}}`. Tests assert `code` only.
126	
127	| Condition | Status | code |
128	|---|---|---|
129	| No route matches the method and path; unknown or foreign slug | 404 | `not_found` |
130	| Missing, malformed or unknown bearer token; bad admin key | 401 | `unauthorized` |
131	| Over the rate limit (adds a `Retry-After` header) | 429 | `rate_limited` |
132	| `Content-Length` > 8192 (the response sets `Connection: close` and the body is not read) | 413 | `payload_too_large` |
133	| Body is not valid UTF-8 JSON, or is not an object | 400 | `invalid_json` |
134	| Schema violation: missing or extra key, wrong type, bad URL, slug, `expires_in` or `now` | 400 | `invalid_request` |
135	| Slug already exists, or is reserved (`healthz`) | 409 | `slug_taken` |
136	| Link expired (E7 only) | 410 | `gone` |
137	| Unhandled exception | 500 | `internal` |
138	
139	Precedence (first failure wins): route 404 → auth 401 → rate limit 429 → size 413 → JSON 400 → validation 400 → resource state 404/409/410.
140	
141	## Acceptance criteria
142	
143	- **AC1 (R1, R15):** `serve --port 0` prints exactly the `LISTENING` line. `GET /healthz` returns 200. SIGINT (or CTRL_BREAK_EVENT on Windows) makes it exit 0 within 5 s.
144	- **AC2 (R2):** E2 with the right key returns 201 and a token matching `^lv_[0-9a-f]{32}$`. With a wrong key it returns 401. The DB holds the SHA-256 of the token, never the plaintext.
145	- **AC3 (R3):** E3, E4 and E5 without a valid bearer token return 401 `unauthorized`.
146	- **AC4 (R4, R5):** E3 without `slug` returns a slug matching `^[a-z0-9]{7}$`. A custom `slug` is echoed back. A repeated slug returns 409. `healthz` and `ab` return 409 and 400 respectively.
147	- **AC5 (R6):** `ftp://x`, `javascript:alert(1)`, `http://`, a URL with a space, and a 2049-character URL each return 400 `invalid_request`.
148	- **AC6 (R7):** `GET /<slug>` returns 302 with the exact `Location`. A later E5 shows `clicks` 1 and `last_clicked_at` set to now.
149	- **AC7 (R8, R12):** With the fake clock at T and `expires_in=60`, the link resolves 302 at T+59 and 410 at T+60. Its clicks stay at the T+59 value.
150	- **AC8 (R9, R10):** Token B gets 404 on E5 and E6 for token A's slug. A's E4 lists only A's links in order. After E6, `GET /<slug>` returns 404 and the slug can be created again.
151	- **AC9 (R11):** With `--rate-limit 3` and the fake clock at a window start plus 10 s, requests 1-3 succeed. Request 4 returns 429 with `Retry-After: 50`. After the clock moves to the next window, the next request succeeds. Redirects are never limited.
152	- **AC10 (R13):** After a restart on the same DB, tokens still authenticate, and links and clicks are unchanged.
153	- **AC11 (R14):** 50 concurrent `GET /<slug>` requests leave `clicks == 50`.
154	- **AC12 (R16):** `shorten` prints the link JSON and exits 0. A 409 makes it exit 1 with empty stdout. An unreachable server makes it exit 3. A missing token makes it exit 2.
155

1	# AGENTS.md — geeky-orchestration
2	
3	Guidance for **any** AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, Windsurf,
4	Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, or an SDK/LangGraph orchestrator) working with this
5	plugin's plan → execute → track workflow. Claude Code reads this via `@AGENTS.md`;
6	most other CLI agents read `AGENTS.md` natively.
7	
8	## Eval operator readiness
9	
10	This section applies only to operators in the source checkout. Contestant exports deliberately omit `evals/`; exported contestants must follow the canonical authorization and exported skills without looking for these operator files or adding a new approval gate. For source-checkout C0 preparation, read [current readiness](evals/c0-readiness.md) and [lessons learned](evals/lessons-learned.md). Generate fresh offline inventory and verify its exact HEAD, source hashes and prompt hash before a separately authorized live action. Local inventory and mock success grant no launch or telemetry publication authority. Preserve historical evidence and scores. Record desired and observed model/effort by role, the authorization reference, attempt/recovery limits, reserve and existing qualification waiver. Once a particular contestant run is authorized, retain the end-to-end workflow permissions already granted by its canonical prompt.
11	
12	## The workflow
13	
14	1. **spec-research** — research and write `feature-specification.md`.
15	2. **geeky-plan** — create the frozen planning package.
16	3. **plan-review** — validate alignment, coverage, sequencing, and readiness.
17	4. **geeky-status** — read-only status and resumption orientation at any packet stage.
18	5. **geeky-implement** — execute Ready tasks with validation and review gates.
19	6. **impl-review** — review delivered code through three domain-specific lanes.
20	7. **archive** — move completed planning artifacts into the archive structure.
21	
22	Use **geeky-orchestrator** when the requested entry point is unclear or when one
23	agent should administer the lifecycle. It examines repository evidence read-only
24	and recommends a workflow before mutation. Clear, explicit requests route to the
25	best matching skill after prerequisite checks. Material ambiguity is clarified;
26	stages are not auto-chained without end-to-end authorization.
27	
28	Full procedures live in the portable Skills under `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
29	
30	## Workflow terminology
31	
32	Use these meanings across skills, briefs and reports. They describe the orchestration
33	domain; retain the target project's own domain language. Existing filenames, schema
34	fields and checkpoint markers remain unchanged.
35	
36	| Term | Meaning |
37	|---|---|
38	| Planning package | Specification, plan, task contracts and tracking artifacts for one approved outcome. "Packet" is an alias; planning folder is its location. |
39	| Workflow stage | A lifecycle activity such as planning, implementation or final implementation review. Numbered "phases" inside a skill are procedure steps, not implementation phases. |
40	| Implementation phase | A group of tasks whose combined requirements are reviewed before advancement. "Wave" means a scheduling group unless the plan explicitly equates it with a phase. |
41	| Task | A bounded unit with an ID, scope, dependencies, acceptance criteria (ACs) and required validation. |
42	| Requirement / AC / Definition of Done | Required outcome or constraint / observable condition for satisfying it / completion conditions for the task. Required tests supply evidence; they do not replace ACs. |
43	| Task contract | The frozen task body and applicable approved requirements. A task brief conveys that contract to a worker. |
44	| Validation | Checks of the work. Validation evidence records what ran or was observed, against which inputs, and the result; a PASS claim alone is not evidence. |
45	| Review | Judgment of evidence against an assigned scope. Task review checks ACs/tests; phase review decides readiness to advance; final implementation review uses `impl-review`. Plan review evaluates the planning package. |
46	| Acceptance | The decision that required outcomes and gates for the stated scope are satisfied. Task Done, phase READY TO ADVANCE and final review PASS have different scopes; none grants release or deployment approval. |
47	| Finding | An evidenced discrepancy. A blocking finding prevents the current contract from being met; an optional improvement is a follow-up. Severity labels retain their review-stage meanings, not an automatic cross-stage mapping. |
48	| Execution batch / review batch | Tasks dispatched together / tasks sharing a reviewer assignment. Each phase has one review batch, the phase review: members wait in In Review until it clears, and each keeps its own verdict. |
49	| Orchestrator / worker / reviewer | Coordinates and accepts work / performs a bounded assignment / evaluates it. `geeky-coder` is the implementation worker; PM describes a planning or phase-review perspective. |
50	
51	## The planning-folder contract
52	
53	**Frozen** (never edit mid-run — they are the contract between plan and implement):
54	`implementation-plan.md`, `feature-specification.md`, `draft.md`, `references.md`,
55	and every `tasks/Tx-*.md` body. If the plan is genuinely wrong, surface it via the
56	kanban **Blocked** lane + `handoff.md` instead of editing the contract.
57	
58	**Mutable** (update continuously during implement):
59	`kanban.md` (single source of truth for lane status), `handoff.md` (running log),
60	and `tasks/Tx-*.notes.md` (per-task notes — these are writable, unlike the task bodies).
61	
62	Record a consequence for another task in that task's notes and in `handoff.md`.
63	
64	## Deterministic quality gates (run these — don't self-report)
65	
66	These replace "I updated the board / the task is done" with fail-stop checks.
67	Every gate: **arguments in, exit 0 = pass / exit 1 = fail, summary on stdout**,
68	optional `--json` / `-Json`. Each ships paired Python + PowerShell with identical
69	behavior. `geeky.manifest.json` is the machine-readable index of the same list.
70	
71	Paths below are relative to this plugin root (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` in Claude Code).
72	Use `python3` where `python` is not on PATH; use `pwsh` (PowerShell 7+) for the `.ps1`.
73	
74	| Gate | When | Python | PowerShell |
75	|---|---|---|---|
76	| Planning-folder valid | start of implement/status | `python scripts/validate-planning-folder.py --path "<folder>"` | `pwsh -File scripts/validate-planning-folder.ps1 -Path "<folder>"` |
77	| Task-file schema | end of plan; start of implement | `python scripts/validate-task-schema.py --path "<folder>"` | `pwsh -File scripts/validate-task-schema.ps1 -Path "<folder>"` |
78	| Kanban integrity | after every lane move | `python scripts/validate-kanban.py --path "<folder>"` | `pwsh -File scripts/validate-kanban.ps1 -Path "<folder>"` |
79	| Definition of Done | in the Done step: move the task to Done, run this gate in the same step, move it back out on failure (D92) | `python scripts/check-dod.py --path "<folder>" --task <ID>` | `pwsh -File scripts/check-dod.ps1 -Path "<folder>" -Task <ID>` |
80	| Commit message | before each commit; pre-planning docs commits use `Tasks: none` | `python scripts/check-commit.py --message "<msg>"` (or `<FILE>`) | `pwsh -File scripts/check-commit.ps1 -Message "<msg>"` (or `<FILE>`) |
81	
82	**Feedback loop:** when a gate exits non-zero, read its output, fix the artifact,
83	and re-run the same gate until it exits 0 before proceeding.
84	
85	## How each agent type runs the gates
86	
87	- **Claude Code:** the frozen-artifact guard fires automatically via
88	  `hooks/hooks.json` (PreToolUse). Run the validators above as explicit steps.
89	- **Other CLI agents (Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, Gemini):** add an
90	  equivalent pre-edit/stop hook in your tool's config pointing at
91	  `hooks/guard-planning-contract.{py,ps1}` (it reads tool-call JSON on stdin,
92	  `--mode block` denies via JSON / exit 2). Invoke the validators as shell steps.
93	- **SDK / graph orchestrators (OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph):** call any validator
94	  with `subprocess.run([...])` inside a guardrail / node; raise a tripwire or
95	  `interrupt()` on a non-zero exit.
96	- **Any MCP-capable agent:** a bundled stdio MCP server (`geeky_mcp`, see `mcp/server.py`,
97	  registered in `.mcp.json`) exposes the gates as tools — `geeky_validate_planning_folder`,
98	  `geeky_validate_task_schema`, `geeky_validate_kanban`, `geeky_check_dod`,
99	  `geeky_check_commit`, `geeky_check_frozen_artifact` — for tool-style invocation with
100	  no per-framework hook config. Run it with `uv run --with "mcp>=1.2.0" python mcp/server.py`
101	  (or `pip install mcp && python mcp/server.py`).
102	
103	## Hard rules for implement
104	
105	Never push to a remote. Never `--no-verify`, `--force`, or `--amend`. Respect each
106	task's declared `Dependencies:`. Stop and finalize state (kanban + handoff) when a
107	task moves to Blocked. Verify task validation evidence against the tested revision,
108	commands and results; a coder's bare PASS claim is insufficient. Reuse valid evidence
109	and record the reason for any rerun. Task review checks ACs and defined tests; one reviewer dispatch at
110	phase end gives each task its verdict and the phase verdict. Phase
111	review checks collective requirements and must return READY TO ADVANCE before the
112	next phase starts; that verdict comes from a reviewer subagent whose agent ID is
113	recorded, and the last phase is included. Final implementation review uses `impl-review`.
114	The orchestrator never edits product code or tests; fixes go to `geeky-coder`. Batch independent
115	work and compatible fixes while preserving each task's verdict and resource isolation.
116

2	
3	Supporting reference for `spec-research` Phase 4. This is a reference template — adapt sections to fit the feature domain; not all sections are required for every spec.
4	
5	```markdown
6	# [Feature Name] Specification
7	
8	**Status:** Not Started
9	**Dependencies:** [prior feature/spec]
10	**Layer:** [Infrastructure / Domain / Security]
11	**Priority:** [Critical Path / Important / Nice-to-have]
12	**Estimated Complexity:** [N tasks across M phases]

15	
16	## 1. Executive Summary
17	## 2. Problem Statement
18	### Current State
19	### Impact of Inaction
20	## 3. Goals & Non-Goals
21	## 4. Architecture
22	## 5. Detailed Design
23	## 6. Cost Estimates (if applicable)
24	## 7. Task Outline (Preliminary)
25	## 8. Risks & Mitigations
26	## 9. Acceptance Criteria
27	## 10. Dependencies on Prior Features
28	## 11. Delegation to Future Specs
29	```
30	
31	Include citations and explicit assumptions at the end of major findings.

1	# Typical research-angle configurations
2	
3	Supporting reference for `spec-research` Phase 2. Pick 3 non-overlapping angles per feature domain.
4	
5	For an infrastructure feature:
6	1. **Codebase Analyst** — audit existing code for dependencies, configuration points, and integration surfaces.
7	2. **Technology Researcher** — web research for current patterns, API versions, pricing models, and recommended practices.
8	3. **Architecture Patterns** — search for deployment patterns, security models, cost optimization, and reliability strategies used by similar systems.
9	
10	For a domain/feature spec:
11	1. **Codebase Analyst** — trace domain boundaries, interfaces, event contracts, and existing patterns.
12	2. **Domain Expert** — research industry best practices, data models, and workflows for the feature domain.
13	3. **Integration Researcher** — identify third-party services, APIs, SDKs, and their latest documentation.
14	
15	For a security/compliance spec:
16	1. **Codebase Analyst** — audit current security posture, auth patterns, secret management, and risk surface.
17	2. **Standards Researcher** — research compliance frameworks (SOC2, GDPR, OWASP), certification requirements, and audit checklists.
18	3. **Tooling Researcher** — research security tooling, scanning services, and policy-as-code integration options.
